questions.title: Why does the sequence-level importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$ use the geometric mean (length normalization) instead of the raw likelihood ratio?
questions.question_body: In Equation (10), the paper defines the importance ratio as $s_{i}(\theta) = \left( \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} (y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}}$. The text explains that without this length normalization, large fluctuations could occur from a few tokens, and ratios for different lengths would require varying clipping ranges. I want to understand the mathematical intuition behind why simply taking the $1/|y_i|$ power solves the variance accumulation problem better than just applying a different clipping bound for long sequences. If I have a sequence of length 100 where one token has a huge probability drop ($w_t \to 0$), how exactly does raising the total product to $1/100$ prevent this single token from destabilizing the entire optimization compared to just bounding $w_t$ directly?

questions.title: How exactly do gradient discrepancies arise from 'expert-activation volatility' in MoE models during GRPO training?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 discusses 'expert-activation volatility' in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. It states that after a gradient update, the routers might activate different experts for the same input compared to the old policy. The text implies this makes token-level importance ratios invalid. However, I am confused about the specific mechanism: if Policy A activates Expert Mix {E1, E2} and Policy B activates Expert Mix {E1, E3}, why does this make comparing $P(A|t)$ and $P(B|t)$ impossible or high-variance? Specifically, in GRPO, we compute $w_{i,t} = P_\theta(y_t|x,y_{<t}) / P_{old}(y_t|x,y_{<t})$. If the active experts define which parameters are used to calculate that probability mass at step $t$, does switching experts mean we are effectively comparing apples to oranges (different parameter subnetworks)? How does GSPO avoid this by looking at whole-sequence probability instead of per-token probabilities from potentially different expert subsets?

questions.title: In GSPO-token, what is the specific purpose of `sg[.]` in defining $s_{i,t}(\theta)$ if numerically it equals 1?
questions.question_body: Equation (15) defines GSPO-token ($s_{i,t}(\theta)$) as: `sg[ s_i(theta) ] * ( pi_theta(...) / sg[ pi_theta(...) ] )`. The paper notes this term evaluates to 1 numerically so GSPO-token reduces to GSPO when advantages are uniform. In standard PPO implementations, `detach` or `sg` is often used within scaling factors to prevent exploding gradients during warmup or specific stability regimes. However, here it seems strictly numerical identity is claimed. Is there a theoretical scenario where token-level advantages ($\widehat{A}_{i,t} \neq \widehat{A}_i$) utilize this token-level importance ratio differently than just re-weighting by the sequence ratio? Or is this variant purely an implementation detail allowing flexibility in adventure assignment without changing the gradient flow direction?

questions.title: Does using sequence-level objectives invalidate backpropagating credit attribution for individual tokens during training?
questions.question_body: The core argument of GSPO is moving from token-level weighting ($w_t$) to sequence-level weighting ($s$). In standard language modeling with soft maximum pooling or cross-entropy loss at every step, backpropagation attributes error gradients to every token proportionally. If GSPO computes a single scalar gradient update based on the derivative of $s_i(\theta) = \exp(\frac{1}{L}\sum \log p_t)$, how does SGD distribute this score among all tokens? Equation (28) shows $\nabla_\theta J = E[...] [ s_i ... * \frac{1}{L}\sum \nabla_\theta \log p_t ]$. This looks like every token still contributes equally to the gradient ($1/L$). But if GRPO clipped certain toxic tokens by reducing their weights significantly ($w_t < 0.8$), while GSPO essentially applies a global scalar clip/scale $s$, isn't riskier information suppression lost? Does switching to sequence-level weighting mean we assume all tokens in a generated response contribute equally to 'badness', losing fine-grained control over specific erroneous parts of a long chain-of-thought?

questions.title: How does sampling responses from the 'old policy' remain stationary enough when traitors effectively render $(x,y)$ pairs stale during large-scale RL?
questions.question_body: "Inference" in RL requires responding samples drawn from an old behavior policy while updating towards a current optimized policy. The paper mentions partitioning batches for memory efficiency but notes "off-policy" risks are managed by importance ratios. However, with sequences of length |y|=2000+, consider that intervening updates change $P(y|x)$ drastically even slightly? If I sample a response under Model V5.0 but optimize towards V5.5+, why don't we hit severe off-policy catastrophes immediately? Does GSPO's claim that 'clipping entire responses' allow larger off-policy deviations fundamentally change how we think about effective batch size versus rlLOM time-step? Specifically, if I generate one example and optimize over it once per epoch due to small batch size constraints, doesn't that require massive KL penalties rather than just clipping?
